The following [[Outline (list)|outline]] is provided as an overview of and topical guide to cryptography:

'''[[Cryptography]]''' (or '''cryptology''') &ndash; practice and study of hiding [[information]]. Modern cryptography intersects the disciplines of [[mathematics]], [[computer science]], and [[engineering]]. Applications of cryptography include [[automated teller machine|ATM cards]], computer passwords, and [[electronic commerce]].

===Modern symmetric-key algorithms===
{{main|Symmetric-key algorithm}}

====[[Stream ciphers]]====
* [[A5/1]] & [[A5/2]] &ndash; ciphers specified for the [[GSM]] cellular telephone standard
* [[BMGL]]
* [[Chameleon (cipher)|Chameleon]]
* [[FISH (cipher)|FISH]] &ndash; by Siemens AG
* [[Fish (cryptography)|WWII 'Fish' cyphers]]
** [[Geheimfernschreiber]] &ndash; WWII mechanical onetime pad by [[Siemens AG]], called [[Sturgeon (cryptography)|STURGEON]] by [[Bletchley Park]]
** [[Pike (cipher)|Pike]] &ndash; improvement on FISH by [[Ross J. Anderson|Ross Anderson]]
** [[Lorenz cipher|Schlusselzusatz]] &ndash; WWII mechanical onetime pad by [[C. Lorenz AG|Lorenz]], called ''tunny'' by [[Bletchley Park]]
* [[HELIX (cipher)|HELIX]]
* [[ISAAC (cipher)|ISAAC]] &ndash; intended as a PRNG
* [[Leviathan (cipher)|Leviathan]]
* [[LILI-128]]
* [[MUGI]] &ndash; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[MULTI-S01]] - [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[One-time pad]] &ndash; Vernam and Mauborgne, patented 1919; an extreme stream cypher
* [[Panama (cipher)|Panama]]
* [[RC4 (cipher)|RC4]] (ARCFOUR) &ndash; one of a series by Professor Ron Rivest of [[MIT]]; [[CRYPTREC]] recommended limited to 128-bit key
** [[CipherSaber]] &ndash; ([[RC4 (cipher)|RC4]] variant with 10 byte random [[Initialization vector|IV]], easy to implement
* [[Salsa20]] &ndash; an [[eSTREAM]] recommended cipher
** [[ChaCha20]] &ndash; A Salsa20 variant.
* [[SEAL (cipher)|SEAL]]
* [[SNOW]]
* [[SOBER]]
** [[SOBER-t16]]
** [[SOBER-t32]]
* [[WAKE (cipher)|WAKE]]

====[[Block ciphers]]====
{{further|Block cipher modes of operation}}
* [[Product cipher]]
* [[Feistel cipher]] &ndash; pattern by [[Horst Feistel]]
* [[Advanced Encryption Standard]] (Rijndael) &ndash; 128-bit block; [[NIST]] selection for the AES, FIPS 197; Created 2001—by [[Joan Daemen]] and [[Vincent Rijmen]]; [[NESSIE]] selection; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation.
* [[Anubis (cipher)|Anubis]] &ndash; 128-bit block
* [[BEAR (cipher)|BEAR]] &ndash; built from a stream cypher and hash function, by [[Ross J. Anderson|Ross Anderson]]
* [[Blowfish (cipher)|Blowfish]] &ndash; 64-bit block; by [[Bruce Schneier]] ''et al.''
* [[Camellia (cipher)|Camellia]] &ndash; 128-bit block; [[NESSIE]] selection (NTT & Mitsubishi Electric); [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[CAST-128]] ([[CAST5]]) &ndash; 64-bit block; one of a series of algorithms by [[Carlisle Adams]] and [[Stafford Tavares]], insistent that the name is not due to their initials
** [[CAST-256]] ([[CAST6]]) &ndash; 128-bit block; the successor to CAST-128 and a candidate for the AES competition
* [[CIPHERUNICORN-A]] &ndash; 128-bit block; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[CIPHERUNICORN-E]] &ndash; 64-bit block; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited)
* [[CMEA (cipher)|CMEA]] &ndash; cipher used in US cellphones, found to have weaknesses.
* [[CS-Cipher]] &ndash; 64-bit block
* [[Data Encryption Standard]] (DES) &ndash; 64-bit block; FIPS 46-3, 1976
* [[DEAL]] &ndash; an AES candidate derived from DES
* [[DES-X]] &ndash; a variant of DES to increase the key size.
* [[FEAL]]
* [[GDES]] &ndash; a [[Data Encryption Standard|DES]] variant designed to speed up encryption
* [[Grand Cru (cipher)|Grand Cru]] &ndash; 128-bit block
* [[Hierocrypt-3]] &ndash; 128-bit block; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[Hierocrypt-L1]] &ndash; 64-bit block; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited)
* [[IDEA NXT]] &ndash; project name FOX, 64-bit and 128-bit block family; Mediacrypt (Switzerland); by [[Pascal Junod]] & [[Serge Vaudenay]] of Swiss Institute of Technology Lausanne
* [[International Data Encryption Algorithm]] (IDEA) &ndash; 64-bit block;[[James Massey]] & [[X Lai]] of [[ETH]] Zurich
* [[Iraqi Block Cipher]] (IBC)
* [[KASUMI (block cipher)|KASUMI]] &ndash; 64-bit block; based on [[MISTY1]], adopted for next generation [[W-CDMA]] [[cellular phone]] security
* [[KHAZAD]] &ndash; 64-bit block designed by Barretto and [[Vincent Rijmen|Rijmen]]
* [[Khufu and Khafre]] &ndash; 64-bit block ciphers
* [[Kuznyechik]] &ndash; Russian 128-bit block cipher, defined in GOST R 34.12-2015 and RFC 7801.
* [[LION (cipher)|LION]] &ndash; block cypher built from stream cypher and hash function, by [[Ross J. Anderson|Ross Anderson]]
* [[LOKI|LOKI89/91]] &ndash; 64-bit block ciphers
* [[LOKI97]] &ndash; 128-bit block cipher, AES candidate
* [[Lucifer (cipher)|Lucifer]] &ndash; by Tuchman ''et al.'' of [[IBM]], early 1970s; modified by [[NSA]]/[[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NBS]] and released as [[Data Encryption Standard|DES]]
* [[MAGENTA]] &ndash; AES candidate
* [[Mars (cipher)|Mars]] &ndash; AES finalist, by [[Don Coppersmith]] et al.
* [[MISTY1]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection 64-bit block; Mitsubishi Electric (Japan); [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited)
* [[MISTY2]] &ndash; 128-bit block: Mitsubishi Electric (Japan)
* [[Nimbus (cipher)|Nimbus]] &ndash; 64-bit block
* [[NOEKEON]] &ndash; 128-bit block
* [[NUSH]] &ndash; variable block length (64-256-bit)
* [[Q (cipher)|Q]] &ndash; 128-bit block
* [[RC2]] &ndash; 64-bit block, variable key length
** [[RC6]] &ndash; variable block length; AES finalist, by [[Ron Rivest]] ''et al.''
** [[RC5]] &ndash; [[Ron Rivest]]
* [[Secure and Fast Encryption Routine|SAFER]] &ndash; variable block length
* [[SC2000]] &ndash; 128-bit block; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[Serpent (cipher)|Serpent]] &ndash; 128-bit block; AES finalist by [[Ross J. Anderson|Ross Anderson]], [[Eli Biham]], [[Lars Ramkilde Knudsen|Lars Knudsen]]
* [[SHACAL-1]] &ndash; 160-bit block
* [[SHACAL-2]] &ndash; 256-bit block cypher; [[NESSIE]] selection Gemplus (France)
* [[Shark (cipher)|Shark]] &ndash; grandfather of [[Rijndael]]/[[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]], by Daemen and Rijmen
** [[Square (cipher)|Square]] &ndash; father of [[Rijndael]]/[[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]], by Daemen and Rijmen
* [[Tiny Encryption Algorithm|TEA]] &ndash; by [[David Wheeler (computer scientist)|David Wheeler]] & [[Roger Needham]]
* [[Triple DES]] &ndash; by [[Walter Tuchman]], leader of the [[Lucifer (cipher)|Lucifer]] design team—not all triple uses of DES increase security, Tuchman's does; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited), only when used as in FIPS Pub 46-3
* [[Twofish]] &ndash; 128-bit block; AES finalist by [[Bruce Schneier]] ''et al.''
* [[XTEA]] &ndash; by [[David Wheeler (computer scientist)|David Wheeler]] & [[Roger Needham]]
* [[3-Way]] &ndash; 96-bit block by [[Joan Daemen]]
* Polyalphabetic substitution machine cyphers
** [[Enigma (machine)|Enigma]] &ndash; WWII German rotor cypher machine—many variants, any user networks for most of the variants
** [[Purple code|Purple]] &ndash; highest security WWII Japanese Foreign Office cypher machine; by Japanese Navy Captain
** [[SIGABA]] &ndash; WWII US cypher machine by [[William Friedman]], [[Frank Rowlett]] ''et al.''
** [[TypeX]] &ndash; WWII UK cypher machine
*Hybrid code/cypher combinations
** [[JN-25]] &ndash; WWII Japanese Navy superencyphered code; many variants
** [[Naval Cypher 3]] &ndash; superencrypted code used by the Royal Navy in the 1930s and into WWII

** [[ECIES-KEM]]

* [[Kyber]]
* [[Merkle–Hellman knapsack cryptosystem]] &ndash; knapsack scheme
* [[McEliece cryptosystem]]
* [[Niederreiter cryptosystem]]
* [[NTRUEncrypt]]
* [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] &ndash; factoring
** [[RSA-KEM]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection asymmetric encryption scheme; ISO/IEC 18033-2 draft
** [[RSA-OAEP]] &ndash; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[Rabin signature]] &ndash; factoring
** [[Rabin-SAEP]]
** [[HIME(R)]]

* [[Threshold cryptosystem]]

==[[Cryptographic hash function]]s==
* [[Message authentication code]]
* [[Keyed-hash message authentication code]]
** Encrypted [[CBC-MAC]] (EMAC) &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection MAC
** [[HMAC]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection MAC; [[ISO/IEC 9797-1]], [[FIPS PUB 113]] and IETF [[Request for Comments|RFC]]
** [[TTMAC]] &ndash; (Two-Track-MAC) NESSIE selection MAC; K.U.Leuven (Belgium) & debis AG (Germany)
** [[UMAC (cryptography)|UMAC]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection MAC; Intel, UNevada Reno, IBM, Technion, & UC Davis
** [[Oblivious Pseudorandom Function]]
* [[MD5]] &ndash; one of a series of message digest algorithms by Prof [[Ron Rivest]] of MIT; 128-bit digest
* [[SHA-1]] &ndash; developed at [[NSA]] 160-bit digest, an FIPS standard; the first released version was defective and replaced by this; NIST/NSA have released several variants with longer 'digest' lengths; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited)
** [[SHA-256]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection hash function, FIPS 180-2, 256-bit digest; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
** [[SHA-384]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection hash function, FIPS 180-2, 384-bit digest; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
** [[SHA-512]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection hash function, FIPS 180-2, 512-bit digest; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation
* [[SHA-3]] &ndash; originally known as Keccak; was the winner of the [[NIST hash function competition]] using [[sponge function]]. 
* [[Streebog]] &ndash; Russian algorithm created to replace an obsolete [[GOST]] hash function defined in obsolete standard GOST R 34.11-94.
* [[RIPEMD-160]] &ndash; developed in Europe for the RIPE project, 160-bit digest; [[CRYPTREC]] recommendation (limited)
* [[RTR0]] &ndash; one of Retter series; developed by [[Maciej A. Czyzewski]]; 160-bit digest
* [[Tiger (hash function)|Tiger]] &ndash; by [[Ross J. Anderson|Ross Anderson]] ''et al.''
* [[Snefru (cryptography)|Snefru]] &ndash; NIST hash function competition
* [[Whirlpool (algorithm)|Whirlpool]] &ndash; [[NESSIE]] selection hash function, Scopus Tecnologia S.A. (Brazil) & K.U.Leuven (Belgium)

==Organizations and selection projects==
===Cryptography standards===
* [[Federal Information Processing Standard]]s (FIPS) Publication Program &ndash; run by [[NIST]] to produce standards in many areas to guide operations of the US Federal government; many FIPS publications are ongoing and related to cryptography
* [[American National Standards Institute]] (ANSI) &ndash; standardization process that produces many standards in many areas; some are cryptography related, ongoing) <!--***we need a list here! -- help, please *** -->
* [[International Organization for Standardization]] (ISO) &ndash; standardization process produces many standards in many areas; some are cryptography related, ongoing <!-- ***we need a list here! -- help, please ***) -->
* [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) &ndash; standardization process produces many standards in many areas; some are cryptography related, ongoing <!-- ***we need a list here! -- help, please ***) -->
* [[Internet Engineering Task Force]] (IETF) &ndash; standardization process that produces many standards called [[Request for Comments|RFCs]]) in many areas; some are cryptography related, ongoing)<!--***we need a list here! -- help, please *** -->

===General cryptographic===
* [[National Security Agency]] (NSA) &ndash; internal evaluation/selections, charged with assisting NIST in its cryptographic responsibilities
* [[Government Communications Headquarters]] (GCHQ) &ndash; internal evaluation/selections, a division is charged with developing and recommending cryptographic standards for the UK government <!-- **** we need more information here -- help! **** -->
* [[Defence Signals Directorate]] (DSD) &ndash; Australian [[SIGINT]] agency, part of [[ECHELON]]
* [[Communications Security Establishment]] (CSE) &ndash; Canadian intelligence agency
<!--*and the same for China, France, Germany, India, Russia, etc-->

===Open efforts===
* [[Data Encryption Standard]] (DES) &ndash; [[NIST|NBS]] selection process, ended 1976
* RIPE &ndash; division of the RACE project sponsored by the [[European Union]], ended mid-1980s
* [[Advanced Encryption Standard]] (AES) &ndash; a "break-off" competition sponsored by [[NIST]], ended in 2001
* [[NESSIE]] Project &ndash; an evaluation/selection program sponsored by the [[European Union]], ended in 2002
* [[eSTREAM]]&ndash; program funded by [[ECRYPT]]; motivated by the failure of all of the [[stream cipher]]s submitted to [[NESSIE]], ended in 2008
* [[CRYPTREC]] &ndash; evaluation/recommendation program sponsored by the Japanese government; draft recommendations published 2003
* [[CrypTool]] &ndash; an e-learning freeware programme in English and German&mdash; exhaustive educational tool about cryptography and cryptanalysis
